 In 1990, a Texas family donated a cave to protect its bats; today, about 4 million female bats use it as a nursery each summer
 SECTIONS In 1990, a Texas family donated a cave to protect its bats; today, about 4 million female bats use it as a nursery each summer By Team Global , Global Desk Last Updated: Nov 05, 2026, 08:00:00 PM IST Rate Story Follow us Share Font Size Abc Small Abc Medium Abc Large Save Print Comment Synopsis A Texas family's vision for conservation transformed their cave into the Eckert James River Bat Cave Preserve in 1990, eschewing fertilizer extraction. Annually, about 4 million female Mexican free-tailed bats find refuge here, utilizing the site as their maternity colony during the crucial breeding season from May to September. Dedicated research and management initiatives strive to protect this critical habitat and deepen understanding of bat population dynamics.
 A bat flies through a mine shaft, highlighting the underground habitats that serve as vital shelters for cave-dwelling bat colonies. (Image credit: Wikimedia Commons)
 For centuries, a cave located in Texas was owned as part of a family property that has been used for some beneficial purpose. It was once a place where bat guano was collected and sold as fertilizer. However, in 1990, the family made a decision that transformed the future of the cave. Instead of exploiting the cave privately, the family donated it for conservation purposes. The Nature Conservancy states that, today, the Eckert James River Bat Cave Preserve has become a protected nursery where about 4 million female Mexican free-tailed bats arrive every summer to give birth and raise their young.
 How a family-owned cave became a bat refuge 
The Eckert family purchased the ranch containing the cave in 1907, and during the early 1900s, W. Phillip Eckert dug out the guano from the cave and sold it as a fertilizer for local farms. However, over time, the family’s relationship with the cave changed. While the site had once provided an economic benefit, later generations recognized that it also supported an extraordinary wildlife colony. 
In 1990, the cave was donated by Richard Phillip Garrett and Virginia Garrett to The Nature Conservancy in memory of their father and grandfather, and the bats are permanently protected. The donation was accompanied by an important condition: the surrounding area would remain open for public enjoyment and education, allowing people to experience the natural event that occurs there every summer. Located in Mason County, Texas, the site now houses one of the largest bat nurseries in the country that provides seasonal shelter to millions of bats reliant on the cave during breeding season.
 A nursery for millions of bats 
 Live Events
 Mexican free-tailed bats gather in a colony, reflecting the large groups that depend on protected caves as seasonal shelters for breeding and raising their young. (Image credit: Wikimedia Commons)
 Every year, the quiet cave changes when Mexican free-tailed bats return for the breeding season. Starting in May, millions of female bats arrive at the preserve and remain there through September. The cave serves as a maternity colony, where many females give birth to a single pup. Young bats remain with their mothers for several weeks until they can fly. By autumn, the colony begins its migration back toward Mexico. The cave is more than a resting place; it is a seasonal nursery where the next generation of the colony begins life.
 Why one cave matters to the ecosystem 
 Mexican free-tailed bats are important for insect control because they eat large numbers of insects while flying at night. These bats help to control agricultural pests by eating insects like moths that harm crops. At night, the colony emerges from the cave and scours the surrounding landscape for food. However, large colonies also create a conservation challenge. When millions of animals depend on one location, disturbance or destruction of that habitat can affect an entire population. The species also has a slow recovery rate because females typically produce only one pup each year. Human disturbance during the maternity season can affect the colony, making careful protection necessary. To preserve the cave for future breeding seasons, conservation partners manage the preserve, monitor bat populations, and limit access during sensitive periods.
 The science behind protecting a bat nursery 
The preserve is also valuable because it provides scientists with a rare opportunity to study one of the world’s largest bat colonies. Researchers monitor the site to understand bat behavior, population changes, and the conditions needed to protect maternity colonies. The cave’s importance extends beyond the bats living inside it, as information collected there can help guide conservation decisions for other bat habitats.
